topic.title: We check the biryani reviews, not the 'SEBI-registered' man
topic.claim: We will read 400 reviews before ordering a mixer-grinder, then hand a stranger crores because he said the words 'SEBI registered'.
topic.behaviour: A Jodhpur FIR described in a thread alleges a man claiming to be SEBI-registered got nearly ₹7 crore for options trading, with a 20% commission on gains promised. The victim, the poster's father, lost ₹1.34 crore. Many families have an older relative who trades or is being 'guided' by someone with a confident voice.
topic.mechanism: Jargon and a claimed registration work as trust shortcuts. Options trading feels like a secret that only insiders can access, and fear of missing out beats the boring step of checking a registration. Shame then keeps families from telling anyone until it's too late.
topic.group: adult children of investing parents, and first-time retail investors
real_details: The thread says an FIR was registered at a Jodhpur police station
The accused allegedly claimed to be SEBI-registered
Nearly ₹7 crore was allegedly handed over for options trading

paragraphs: Papa reads every review before buying a mixer-grinder. Then hands a stranger crores because he said 'SEBI registered'. So why does that work?
An FIR in Jodhpur alleges exactly this.
A man allegedly claimed to be SEBI-registered. He allegedly got nearly ₹7 crore for options trading, with a 20% commission on gains promised.
The mixer-grinder is easy to doubt. You can see it, touch it, return it.
Options trading feels different. It sounds like a room only insiders get into.
And the man at the door seems to know the password.
"SEBI registered" is that password. Few ask to see it.
SEBI itself has warned that more and more entities falsely claim to be registered. It keeps telling investors to verify.
But checking feels boring. Missing out feels worse.
The darker part comes after the money goes.
Papa says nothing. Mummy doesn't know. The family WhatsApp group gets good morning messages as usual.
Often he keeps waiting for one good month to fix it. That waiting is where the real damage happens.
Your papa will still call you before buying a mixer-grinder.
Nobody calls before handing over crores. You call first.

draft.caption: My parents will haggle over a ₹50 delivery fee and trust a stranger with a confident voice on the phone
draft.alt_text: A six-slide text carousel about how Indian parents carefully research small purchases but trust strangers claiming to be SEBI-registered with large investments. It cites a Jodhpur FIR alleging a man got nearly ₹7 crore for options trading with a 20% commission promised, where one father lost ₹1.34 crore, notes SEBI's warning that entities falsely claim registration, and ends by urging adult children to call their parents first.

hook_candidates.hook: Papa reads every review before buying a mixer-grinder. Then hands a stranger crores because he said 'SEBI registered'. So why does that work?
In most Indian homes, a mixer-grinder gets more checking than a crore of rupees. And I know how that sounds.
There's something strange about how Indian dads check things. A mixer-grinder gets every review read. A stranger asking for crores gets none.
Dear Papa, you read every review before buying a mixer-grinder. Why didn't you call anyone before handing a stranger crores?
In Jodhpur, one father allegedly lost ₹1.34 crore. He didn't lose it to a bad trade. He lost it to two words.
